Listening.transcript:
[Part 1]
You will hear a phone conversation between a receptionist and a new member joining a community sports centre. First you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10. The caller's surname is spelled Halloway. The membership type requested is the family package. The annual fee for this package is £245. The centre is located on Fenwick Road. New members receive a free induction session on Tuesday. The locker deposit required is £15. The pool opening time on weekdays is 6 am. Members must renew their photo ID every 2 years. The caller's preferred contact number ends in 3390. The confirmation email will be sent within 24 hours.

[Part 2]
You will hear a council officer explaining a new recycling scheme to residents. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20. The new scheme starts on the first day of March. Food waste should be placed in the brown caddy. Garden waste is collected every two weeks. Glass bottles must be taken to the drop-off point on Mill Lane. The recycling hotline number ends in 7124. Residents who contaminate bins receive a written warning. The officer explained that the council introduced the scheme mainly to meet a national recycling target set for next year. For a replacement bin, the officer said residents should visit the council website rather than phoning the hotline. Large furniture items are only collected by appointment, the officer confirmed, and cannot simply be left out. The trial phase, she said, would run for six months before being reviewed by the council.

[Part 3]
You will hear two students, Maya and Josh, discussing a research project on urban trees. First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30. They plan to survey 12 streets across the city. Their supervisor recommended they focus on trees planted after 2010. The final report is due in eight weeks. Josh will contact the parks department for planting records. Maya will design a short questionnaire for residents. They need approval from the ethics committee before starting. Maya said she first became interested after reading about it in a journal article her sister sent her. Josh admitted his main concern was getting access to the council's tree-planting data in time. Both agreed that the survey method was the strongest part of the proposal so far. Maya suggested that before anything else they should revise the questionnaire based on their supervisor's comments.

[Part 4]
You will hear part of a lecture on the history of the tea trade. First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Tea was first traded internationally along the maritime routes. By the seventeenth century, tea had become popular in Europe. The lecturer states that tea was originally valued for its medicinal properties. Large-scale plantations were later established in India. The introduction of the steamship reduced shipping time to under 60 days. A new grading system for leaf quality was introduced in 1870. Auctions moved from London to Mombasa in the twentieth century. Today the largest producer by volume is China. The lecturer notes that tea consumption per person is highest in Turkey. The lecture concludes by mentioning a rise in demand for specialty tea.

passages.title: The Rise of Urban Beekeeping
passages.text: Over the past two decades, beekeeping has moved from rural farms into the heart of many cities. Rooftops, balconies and community gardens now host thousands of hives in urban centres worldwide. The first recorded urban apiary in the modern movement was established on a rooftop in 1983. A single healthy hive can contain up to 60000 bees during summer. Urban beekeepers commonly harvest honey two times per year. One frequently cited advantage of city hives is access to a wider variety of flowering plants. Local regulations in many cities now require hives to be set back at least 3 metres from public paths. Community groups often host beginner courses lasting four weekends. Some ecologists caution that packing too many hives into a small area can crowd out wild, native pollinator species that compete for the same flowers. In response, several city councils have introduced registration schemes so that hive locations can be tracked and disputes resolved. The passage does not state why urban beekeeping began, only where and when the modern movement started. Requirements vary widely between cities, and no universal training requirement is described in the passage. Because rooftops absorb more heat during the day, hives placed there can run noticeably warmer than hives kept at ground level. The passage discusses hive density and regulation but gives no comparison of honey prices between urban and rural sources. Community groups often host beginner courses lasting four weekends, giving newcomers hands-on experience before they keep their own hive.

passages.title: Sleep and Memory Consolidation
passages.text: Researchers have long observed a link between sleep and the ability to retain newly learned information. Recent laboratory studies have begun to clarify exactly how this process, known as memory consolidation, works. In one widely cited study, participants who slept recalled 20 percent more word pairs than those who stayed awake. The stage of sleep most associated with memory consolidation is called slow-wave sleep. Researchers used EEG recordings to observe brain activity during sleep. The study involved 48 adult participants in total. A short nap of only 90 minutes produced a measurable improvement in recall. The researchers propose that memories are transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex during sleep. Sleep deprivation for a single night reduced recall accuracy by roughly 30 percent. The study set out specifically to investigate how sleep supports the retention of newly learned material. The stage of sleep most associated with memory consolidation is called slow-wave sleep, during which the brain appears to reorganise recent experiences. The researchers propose that memories are transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex during sleep for longer-term storage. The passage states only the total number of adult participants, not their occupation or student status. A short nap of only ninety minutes produced a measurable improvement in recall compared with staying awake. Sleep deprivation for a single night reduced recall accuracy by roughly thirty percent, showing a clear measurable effect. The passage reports the effect of a short nap but does not compare it directly with a full night's sleep.

passages.title: Automation and the Future of Craft Professions
passages.text: As robotics and machine learning extend into fields once considered safe from automation, commentators increasingly ask whether skilled manual trades and craft professions will endure the next wave of technological change. A recent survey found that 42 percent of master furniture makers reported using computer-guided tools for at least part of their work. The report estimates that fully automated systems can currently replicate around 70 percent of the physical motions used in traditional joinery. Craft apprenticeships in the surveyed region declined by 15 percent over the past decade. One workshop owner interviewed had trained apprentices for over 30 years. The author argues that value increasingly lies in customisation rather than pure production speed. While acknowledging real disruption, the author remains cautiously optimistic that craft trades can adapt rather than disappear. The workshop owner argued that automation, used selectively, frees up time for the more creative and judgement-based parts of the craft. Only 42 percent reported using computer-guided tools for at least part of their work, far from all makers relying entirely on automation. The report estimates automated systems can replicate around 70 percent of physical motions, not all aspects of the craft. Craft apprenticeships in the surveyed region declined by 15 percent over the past decade. The passage discusses value shifting toward customisation but does not report a trend in consumer demand levels. One workshop owner interviewed had trained apprentices for over thirty years, well beyond two decades. The author remains cautiously optimistic that craft trades can adapt rather than disappear, contradicting this statement.

questions.prompt: The chart below shows the percentage of households in a small city using four different heating fuels in 1995 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
questions.modelAnswer:
The chart compares the share of households using gas, electricity, oil and solar heating in 1995 and 2020. Overall, gas remained the most common fuel in both years, but its share fell considerably, while solar heating grew from a marginal option into a major source.

In 1995, just over half of households relied on gas, with electricity and oil each supplying a fifth of homes and solar heating used by only a small minority. By 2020, gas use had dropped to around a third of households, and oil usage halved to about a tenth. In contrast, electricity rose moderately, and solar heating increased fivefold to become the second most common fuel.

Overall, the data indicate a clear shift away from oil and, to a lesser extent, gas, toward renewable and electrical alternatives over the twenty-five-year period.

questions.prompt: Some people think that governments should invest primarily in public transport rather than roads for private cars. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
questions.modelAnswer:
Public spending on transport infrastructure is a recurring policy debate, and I largely agree that prioritising public transport over road expansion produces better long-term outcomes for cities.

Firstly, investment in buses, trams and railways tends to reduce congestion more effectively than building additional roads. Widening a motorway often encourages more people to drive, a phenomenon known as induced demand, so the initial relief from congestion is frequently temporary. By contrast, a reliable rail network can shift large numbers of commuters away from private cars permanently.

Secondly, public transport investment brings environmental benefits. Buses and trains typically emit far less carbon dioxide per passenger than private vehicles, particularly when powered by electricity. Given the urgency of reducing emissions, channelling limited public funds toward low-carbon transport seems a more responsible use of resources than expanding road capacity for private cars.

However, road investment cannot be dismissed entirely. Rural communities, where public transport is often impractical due to low population density, still depend heavily on private vehicles and well-maintained roads. Ignoring this need risks leaving rural residents isolated.

In conclusion, while a balanced approach is necessary, I believe governments should direct the majority of transport funding toward public transport, since it addresses congestion and emissions more sustainably than expanding roads for private cars.
